evidence.excerpt: Sauti said, 'O Brahmana, Chyavana, the son of Bhrigu, begot a son in the womb of his wife Sukanya. And that son was the illustrious Pramati of resplendent energy.
And Pramati begot in the womb of Ghritachi a son called Ruru. And Ruru begot on his wife Pramadvara a son called Sunaka.
Formerly there was a great Rishi called Sthulakesa possessed of ascetic power and learning and kindly disposed towards all creatures.
Viswavasu, the King of the Gandharvas, it is said, had intimacy with Menaka, the celestial dancing-girl.
And the Apsara, Menaka, O thou of the Bhrigu race, when her time was come, brought forth an infant near the hermitage of Sthulakesa.

And he perceived that it was a female child, bright as the offspring of an Immortal and blazing, as it were, with beauty: And the great Brahmana, Sthulakesa, the first of Munis, seeing that female child, and filled with compassion, took it up and reared it.
And because she surpassed all of her sex in goodness, beauty, and every quality, the great Rishi called her by the name of Pramadvara.
And the pious Ruru having seen Pramadvara in the hermitage of Sthulakesa became one whose heart was pierced
by the god of love.
And Ruru by means of his companions made his father Pramati, the son of Bhrigu, acquainted with his passion.
And Pramati demanded her of the far-famed Sthulakesa for his son. And her foster-father betrothed the virgin Pramadvara to Ruru
the beautiful virgin while at play with companions of her own sex, her time having come, impelled by fate, trod upon a serpent which she did not perceive as it lay in coil.
And the reptile, urged to execute the will of Fate, violently darted its envenomed fangs into the body of the heedless maiden.
And then there came many noted Brahmanas filled with compassion, and they sat around her.

And Swastyatreya, Mahajana, Kushika, Sankhamekhala, Uddalaka, Katha, and Sweta of great renown, Bharadwaja, Kaunakutsya, Arshtishena, Gautama, Pramati, and Pramati's son Ruru, and other inhabitants of the forest, came there.
a messenger from heaven came to him in the forest and addressed him thus
And the celestial messenger said unto Ruru, 'Resign half of thy own life to thy bride, and then, O Ruru of the race of Bhrigu, thy Pramadvara shall rise from the ground.
Then the king of Gandharvas (the father of Pramadvara) and the celestial messenger, both of excellent qualities, went to the god Dharma (the Judge of the dead) and addressed him, saying,
If it be thy will, O Dharmaraja, let the amiable Pramadvara, the betrothed wife of Ruru, now lying dead, rise up with a moiety of Ruru's life.
And Dharmaraja answered, 'O messenger of the gods, if it be thy wish, let Pramadvara, the betrothed wife of Ruru, rise up endued with a moiety of Ruru's life.
And on an auspicious day their fathers gladly married them with due rites. And the couple passed their days, devoted to each other. And Ruru having obtained such a wife
And there he saw an old serpent of the Dundubha species lying stretched on the ground.
And Ruru thereupon lifted up in anger his staff, even like to the staff of Death
And the Rishi Ruru hearing these words of the serpent, and seeing that it was bewildered with fear, albeit a snake of the Dundubha species, killed it not.
And the Dundubha replied, 'O Ruru! I was formerly a Rishi by name Sahasrapat. And it is by the curse of a Brahmana that I have been transformed into a snake.
In former times, I had a friend Khagama by name. He was impetuous in his speech and possessed of spiritual power by virtue of his austerities.

On recovering his senses, that truth-telling and vow-observing ascetic, burning with wrath, exclaimed, 'Since thou hast made a powerless mock snake to frighten me, thou shalt be turned even into a venomless serpent thyself by my curse.
O pious one! when Ruru the pure son of Pramati, will appear, thou shall be delivered from the curse the moment thou seest him. Thou art the very Ruru and the son of Pramati.
And that illustrious man and the best of Brahmanas then left his snake-body, and attained his own form and original brightness.
A Brahmana should be versed in the Vedas and Vedangas, and should inspire all creatures with belief in God.
why was king Janamejaya bent upon destroying the serpents?--And why and how were they saved by the wise Astika?
Regaining consciousness, he came home and asked his father to relate the history in question. Thus asked, his father related all about the story.
For what reason did that tiger among kings, the royal Janamejaya, determine to take the lives of the snakes by means of a sacrifice?
Whose son was that monarch who celebrated the snake-sacrifice?
Saunaka said, 'I am desirous of hearing at length the charming story of that Rishi, that illustrious Brahmana named Astika.
Sauti said, 'This history (first) recited by Krishna-Dwaipayana, is called a Purana by the Brahmanas. It was formerly narrated by my wise father, Lomaharshana, the disciple of Vyasa

The father of Astika was powerful like Prajapati. He was a Brahma-charin, always engaged in austere devotions. He ate sparingly, was a great ascetic, and had his lust under complete control. And he was known by the name of Jaratkaru.
Who are you thus hanging heads down in this hole by a rope of virana fibres that is again secretly eaten into on all sides by a rat living here?
Thereupon Vasuki rose and offered his sister for the Rishi's acceptance.
Then that Rishi of great wisdom and austere penances asked him, saying, 'Tell me truly what is the name of this thy sister, O snake.
Vasuki replied, 'O Jaratkaru, this my younger sister is called Jaratkaru. Given away by me, accept this slender-waisted damsel for thy spouse.
Saying this, he offered his beautiful sister to Jaratkaru who then espoused her with ordained rites.

Sauti said, 'O foremost of persons acquainted with Brahma, the mother of the snakes had cursed them of old, saying, 'He that hath the Wind for his charioteer (viz., Agni) shall burn you all in Janamejaya's sacrifice!

It was to neutralise that curse that the chief of the snakes married his sister to that high-souled Rishi of excellent vows. The Rishi wedded her according to the rites ordained (in the scriptures), and from them was born a high-souled son called Astika.
Astika delivered the Nagas, viz., his brothers and maternal uncles and other snakes (from a fiery death).
O Brahmana, in the golden age, Prajapati had two daughters. O sinless one, the sisters were endowed with wonderful beauty. Named Kadru and Vinata, they became the wives of Kasyapa.
Kasyapa derived great pleasure from his two wedded wives and being gratified he, resembling Prajapati himself, offered to give each of them a boon.

Kadru wished to have for sons a thousand snakes all of equal splendour. And Vinata wished to bring forth two sons surpassing the thousand offsprings of Kadru in strength, energy, size of body, and prowess.
Unto Kadru her lord gave that boon about a multitude of offspring. And unto Vinata also, Kasyapa said, 'Be it so!
Kadru also obtained her thousand sons of equal splendour.
after a long time, Kadru brought forth a thousand eggs, and Vinata two.
Five hundred years passed away, and the thousand eggs produced by Kadru burst and out came the progeny. But the twins of Vinata did not appear.

Vinata was jealous, and therefore she broke one of the eggs and found in it an embryo with the upper part developed but the lower one undeveloped. At this, the child in the egg became angry and cursed his mother
Thus cursing his mother, the child rose to the sky. O Brahmana, even he is the charioteer of Surya, always seen in the hour of morning!
Then at the expiration of the five hundred years, bursting open the other egg, out came Garuda, the serpent-eater.
immediately on seeing the light, that son of Vinata left his mother.
And the lord of birds, feeling hungry, took wing in quest of the food assigned to him by the Great Ordainer of all.

Sauti said, 'O ascetic, about this time the two sisters saw approaching near, that steed of complacent appearance named Uchchaihsravas who was worshipped by the gods, that gem of steeds, who arose at the churning of the Ocean for nectar.
Divine, graceful, perpetually young, creation's master-piece, and of irresistible vigour, it was blest with every auspicious mark.
Saunaka asked, 'Why did the gods churn the Ocean for nectar, and under what circumstances and when as you say, did that best of steeds so powerful and resplendent spring?

unresolved: Page 25 says Chyavana begot Pramati in Sukanya's womb; page 26 calls Pramati the son of Bhrigu. Both paternal claims are retained as disputed without reconciling the differing descriptions.
Sunaka and Saunaka remain distinct because this batch does not establish their identity.
Krishna-Dwaipayana and Vyasa remain distinct because this batch does not explicitly establish that they identify the same individual.
The unnamed mother of the snakes on page 29 is not explicitly identified as Kadru.

Brahma may denote a spiritual concept rather than an individual. Fate and Death may be personifications, and the reference to belief in God does not establish a particular individual identity. These records remain provisional.
The batch does not establish identities among God, the Great Ordainer, Prajapati, Brahma, Dharma, Death, or Fate.
Dundubha is explicitly a species designation. It is retained in Sahasrapat's description rather than treated as an established personal alias.
Astika's birth from the two Jaratkarus establishes parentage; its parenthood mode is left unspecified.
Kasyapa is explicitly the husband of Kadru and Vinata and grants offspring boons, but the batch does not directly identify him as the parent of Garuda or Vinata's unnamed first son.

Kadru's thousand snake sons, Jaratkaru's hanging ancestors, Astika's brothers and maternal uncles, companions, maid-servants, and unspecified offspring are not individually differentiated. No additional individuals or pairwise family relationships are created from these group references.
The passage concerning Astika's brothers and maternal uncles does not individually identify an additional sibling or uncle, and does not state Kadru's parentage of Vasuki or Vasuki's sister.
Vinata's two children are explicitly called twins, supporting their sibling relationship independently of their shared parentage.

matches.reason: The existing record explicitly identifies Ugrasrava as Sauti and Lomaharshana's son; the current narrator names Lomaharshana as his father.
Both occur as Saunaka in the framing dialogue with Sauti, asking him to recount the epic's histories.
Both explicitly identify Bhrigu as Chyavana's parent.
The same genealogy identifies Chyavana as Bhrigu's son, Sukanya's husband, and Pramati's parent.
Both identify Sukanya as Chyavana's wife, in whose womb Pramati was begotten.
Both give the same genealogy: Pramati is begotten by Chyavana in Sukanya's womb and begets Ruru in Ghritachi's womb.
Both identify Ghritachi as the individual in whose womb Pramati begot Ruru.
Both identify Ruru through Pramati and Ghritachi, his wife Pramadvara, and their son Sunaka.
Both identify the female child reared and named by Sthulakesa, subsequently Ruru's wife and Sunaka's mother.
Both explicitly identify Sunaka as the son begotten by Ruru on his wife Pramadvara.
Both identify the Rishi who reared the abandoned female child and named her Pramadvara.
Both identify Viswavasu as King of the Gandharvas who had intimacy with Menaka.
Both identify the Apsara and celestial dancing-girl associated with Viswavasu who gives birth near Sthulakesa's hermitage.
The name is corroborated by the distinctive judicial divine role: the existing god of justice and the current god designated Judge of the dead.
Both identify the king of the snake-sacrifice; the current destruction of snakes distinguishes him from the other Janamejaya records.
Both identify the subject of the explicitly named Astika story in the Bharata: the existing introductory reading reference and the current framing introduction to that history.

Existing evidence explicitly names Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa and identifies Dwaipayana as the Purana's first promulgator; the current passage identifies Krishna-Dwaipayana as this history's first reciter.
Both explicitly identify Lomaharshana as the father of the narrator Sauti/Ugrasrava.

Existing evidence explicitly joins the names Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa and places Sauti's father reading the Bharata with Krishna-Dwaipayana. This corroborates the current Lomaharshana-as-disciple context and resolves the two local names as one established identity.
The existing synopsis specifically locates Garuda's birth in Astika; the current Astika Parva passage narrates Garuda emerging from Vinata's other egg.
